strengths: Theoretically grounded approach with rigorous analysis of joint entropy bounds via Lemma 1 and connections to mutual information decay through Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi correlation coefficient
Broad practical applicability as an inference-only, training-free method that works as a drop-in replacement for any MDLM without architectural modification

Comprehensive experimental validation across three model families (LLaDA, Dream, DiffuCoder), six benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP, BBH, MMLU-Pro), and multiple speedup factors with consistent improvements (up to 27% on math, 20% on code)
Insightful ablation study (Section 4.4) demonstrating that random scheduling benefits significantly from dilated-incremental patterns, validating theoretical claims about mutual information reduction
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and thorough experimental details enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Strong theoretical assumptions (fast-mixing first-order Markov chain) are not empirically validated; natural language exhibits long-range dependencies violating first-order Markov property, and the practical impact of assumption violations is unquantified

Limited baseline comparisons: only self-confidence baselines tested; missing direct comparisons to concurrent schedulers (Path Planning, EB-Sampler) mentioned in related work, weakening claims of superiority

Confounded experimental design: DUS uses incremental k schedule while confidence baseline uses fixed k = log₂B; main results don't isolate this contribution, though Table 3 partial ablation addresses this only on 300 GSM8K samples

Skip mechanism (Section 3.6) lacks formal integration into algorithm, missing hyperparameter specification (threshold values), and is never ablated experimentally despite appearing to be a significant practical component
Modest improvements on general knowledge benchmarks (BBH: 1-5%, MMLU-Pro: 5-9%) suggest domain-dependent applicability not discussed; code results also show degradation at high speedups (B=64)

No computational cost analysis beyond NFE: wall-clock time, memory usage, and latency comparisons absent; different scheduling patterns may have different parallelization efficiency and cache behavior
Theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis applies to single blocks, but semi-AR setup processes blocks sequentially with unanalyzed inter-block interactions and global coherence effects

Experimental protocol details underspecified: early stopping implementation analyzed insufficiently; counterintuitive result of DiffuCoder base outperforming instruct variant under DUS lacks explanation

strengths: Practical inference-only method that requires no model retraining and can be applied to existing MDLMs
Consistent empirical improvements across multiple models (LLaDA, Dream, DiffuCoder) and benchmarks, with substantial gains on math tasks (up to 27%)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning math, code, and general knowledge benchmarks with systematic speedup analysis
Clear algorithmic description with concrete examples and ablation studies isolating different components
Addresses a relevant problem in making diffusion language models competitive with autoregressive approaches
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis relies on unrealistic first-order Markov assumption for language with complex long-range dependencies; no empirical validation of fast-mixing property (ρ < 1) or characterization of distance threshold D needed for bounds to hold
Skip mechanism (deferring tokens based on confidence) directly violates fixed-spacing assumption underlying Lemma 1 and undermines theoretical guarantees, yet is not well-integrated into the analysis

Weak baseline comparisons: primary comparison is only to confidence-based planning; missing comparisons to EB-Sampler, Path Planning (P2), KV-caching methods, and other recent acceleration techniques mentioned in related work

Experimental design issues: inconsistent NFE budgets across planners (dilated-incremental k vs. fixed k in ablations), ablation study uses only 300 samples (23% of dataset) with no statistical significance testing, making it difficult to assess true contribution

Insufficient explanation of empirical success: unclear why spacing tokens improves quality (richer context? reduced error propagation?); unexplained phenomena (e.g., base models outperform instruction-tuned on code despite DUS, larger gains on math than code) suggest incomplete understanding

Limited baseline strength in Table 3: random + dilated scheduling achieves 61.33% vs. DUS 71.67% on GSM8K—only 10 points difference—suggesting spacing is more important than the planner itself, which contradicts theoretical emphasis on entropy minimization

Incomplete analysis: no sensitivity to dilation base a, unclear contribution of skip mechanism, no characterization of when/why DUS works best (math vs. code, base vs. instruction-tuned), limited to 7-8B models only
Comparison to AR models only qualitative (dashed lines): quantitative gaps at high speedups not reported; unclear if DUS closes the fundamental efficiency gap with autoregressive baselines

strengths: Inference-only, model-agnostic method requiring no retraining; immediately deployable as a drop-in replacement across multiple MDLM architectures
Logarithmic complexity reduction (O(B) → O(log B)) with substantial empirical speedups (up to 10.7×) and consistent improvements (up to 27% on math benchmarks)
Theoretical analysis via Lemmas 1-2 providing formal justification for why DUS achieves joint entropy bounds that confidence-based planners lack
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 models and 6 benchmarks with proper ablation studies (Section 4.4) validating design choices
Rare speed-quality trade-off where the method achieves both faster inference and better accuracy simultaneously, with clear qualitative examples (Figure 1)
Strong presentation with clear motivation, well-designed figures, and generally accessible writing
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Core theoretical analysis assumes fast-mixing first-order Markov chain, but these assumptions are neither empirically validated nor likely to hold for language with known long-range dependencies; no measurement of actual MI decay or verification of spacing bounds in real models
Skip mechanism (Section 3.6) mentioned as important but never formally defined—no threshold values, frequency analysis, or evaluation of how it affects spacing guarantees

Circular reasoning on independence (Eq. 3→4): Paper claims tokens are 'unmasked independently' to justify summing entropies, yet Lemma 2 bounds non-zero MI between tokens; this contradiction needs clarification
Limited baseline comparisons: Only compared against self-confidence in main results; missing comparisons with EB-Sampler, Path Planning (P2), and other recent planners except in limited ablations
Block merging operation (Eq. 7) when |P_R| < |P_{R-1}| could violate claimed spacing guarantees; no analysis of its impact on theoretical bounds

Incomplete mechanism analysis: No sensitivity analysis for dilation base a (only a=2 tested); no investigation of failure modes where method hurts performance (e.g., DiffuCoder-Instruct HumanEval at B=64)
Unjustified connection between entropy minimization and downstream task performance; paper assumes this coupling without explicit justification or alternative objectives comparison
Limited scope: All experiments use semi-AR with blocks B∈{8,16,32,64}; unclear how DUS scales to fully parallel generation, larger blocks, or beyond 7-8B models
Reproducibility gaps: No code release mentioned, skip mechanism thresholds undocumented, model-specific confidence measures not fully detailed

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear explanation of why existing confidence-based planners fail to exploit parallelism in masked diffusion models
Rigorous theoretical framework deriving the entropy gap minimization principle (Lemma 3.3, Corollary 3.4) with formal guarantees under fast-mixing assumptions (Lemmas 3.5-3.6)
Practical inference-only method requiring no model retraining or architecture modifications, applicable as drop-in planner or post-filter
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 MDLM variants and 6 diverse benchmarks with consistent improvements (up to 27% on math, 20% on code, 5.8× wall-clock speedup)
Extensive ablation studies and analysis including block size effects, skip threshold tuning, parameter sensitivity, runtime breakdown, and token distance validation
Strong demonstration of complementarity: dilated spacing improves adaptive samplers (EB/CB) by up to 13.4% without modifying core selection logic
Honest discussion of theoretical limitations (late iterations, strong dependencies) with empirical evidence that DUS works despite theory-practice gap
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Assumptions 3.1 (optimal estimator) and 3.2 (planner objective) are strong ideals; gap between learned denoisers and assumptions is not analyzed. Fast-mixing VLMC assumption is violated in code/poetry with strong global constraints
Theoretical guarantees primarily apply to early iterations where fewest tokens are unmasked; late-iteration behavior relies on heuristic justification rather than rigorous analysis

Modest improvements on general-knowledge tasks (BBH: +1-5%, MMLU-Pro: +5-9%) and severe accuracy drops at extreme speedups (e.g., HumanEval LLaDA-Base: 34.76%→6.71% at 10.7×), contradicting claim that method both accelerates and enhances quality

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Appendix B.9 shows EB/CB samplers achieve higher accuracy than DUS at higher NFE. DUS occupies only the lowest-NFE operating point; limited comparison with recent methods (P2, JYS dismissed due to model scale)
Limited experimental scope: restricted to 7-8B models where inference efficiency matters less; no evaluation at larger scales (13B+, 70B+) where efficiency gains are most valuable
Parameter choices lack strong justification: base a=2 is fixed and justified only empirically (Appendix B.4); choice of k=log₂B appears arbitrary; optimal skip threshold c is task-dependent

Presentation issues: critical results relegated to appendices (wall-clock speedup in B.8); dense main paper; notation inconsistencies; connection between entropy gap and practical performance could be more intuitive
Early stopping results (Figure 2) show DUS underperforms adaptive methods, suggesting unsuitability for latency-constrained scenarios; method only applies to semi-AR block-wise inference

strengths: Clear problem formulation and practical motivation for accelerating masked diffusion inference
Theoretically grounded approach with entropy gap minimization providing intuition for the spacing-based design
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (LLaDA, Dream, DiffuCoder) and diverse benchmarks (math, code, reasoning, instruction-following)
Practical inference-only method requiring no model retraining or architectural modifications
Consistent improvements over confidence-based planners (5-27% gains on math/code), achieving up to 5.8× wall-clock speedup
Extensive ablations and analysis including token distance metrics, parameter sensitivity, and design justification
Complementary hybrid extension showing dilated spacing improves adaptive samplers (EB/CB) as post-filter
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: fast-mixing VLMC assumption is acknowledged to be violated on code and constrained domains, yet method is applied without rigorous justification for when theoretical guarantees hold

Limited novelty: the core insight that spacing reduces conditional dependencies is well-established; applying it via logarithmic schedule is straightforward engineering without clear theoretical justification for why logarithmic base-2 specifically

Weak baseline comparisons: main competitor is self-confidence planners; limited comparison with adaptive samplers (EB/CB) which achieve higher accuracy at higher NFE; no comparison with Path Planning (P2) or learning-based scheduling methods

Theory does not fully justify design: entropy gap minimization motivates spacing but not the specific schedule in Eq. (8)-(9); design parameters (a=2, base_skip=1) emerge empirically from ablations; skip heuristic contradicts 'model-agnostic' claims
Inconsistent experimental results: MBPP shows less smooth trends due to low accuracy at high speedups; wall-clock speedup (3.9-5.8×) lags behind NFE speedup improvements, suggesting overhead issues

Block size B introduced as free tuning parameter with no principled selection method; users must manually tune B for desired quality-speed tradeoff without clear guidance

Limited experimental scope: only 7-8B models evaluated; unclear if patterns hold at larger scales; fully parallel regime (B=G) shows 28-51× speedup with severe accuracy loss, making regime selection unclear

Theoretical analysis has gaps: fast-mixing VLMC assumptions cannot be verified in practice; bounds depend on unknown mixing rates; no finite-sample analysis; Lemma 3.3 is standard chain rule entropy decomposition

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation grounded in information theory (entropy gap minimization with formal bounds Lemmas 3.3-3.6)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 MDLM variants, 4+ benchmarks with consistent improvements (up to 27% on math/code over confidence baseline)
Inference-only method with zero modifications to model training or architecture; broad applicability across diverse models and tasks
Practical value demonstrated through wall-clock speedups (3.9-5.8×) and deterministic, controllable latency via block size B
Thorough ablations and reproducibility support (Appendices B.1-B.9, promised code release) enabling detailed analysis of design choices
Novel position-based (non-model-dependent) scheduling principle orthogonal to adaptive samplers; can enhance EB/CB methods
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1, 4, 5) and qualitative generation trajectories illustrating spacing principle
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: optimal estimator assumption (Assumption 3.1) doesn't hold for learned denoisers; impact on bound tightness not quantified
VLMC fast-mixing assumption violated on code/reasoning tasks; distinction between full and 'block-level' fast-mixing is informal
Late-iteration analysis relies on heuristic reasoning (richer context helps) rather than formal guarantees; bounds are most informative early only
Inconsistent improvements across tasks: modest gains on general knowledge (BBH +1-5%, MMLU +5-9%) vs. strong gains on math; mechanism unclear
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Path Planning (P2) and Jump Your Steps (JYS) mentioned but not empirically compared; semi-AR block diffusion trade-offs not addressed
Generalization questions: all experiments use semi-AR blocks; single-block (B=G) regime shows low accuracy; scale to 13B+ models untested

Design choices lack principled justification: base a=2 appears arbitrary (Appendix B.4 shows alternatives degrade but no rationale); skip threshold recommendation contradicts ablations (Table 7 shows c=0.3 improves some tasks)
Persistent quality gap to autoregressive models: GSM8K 57% vs 88.5%, HumanEval 11.6% vs 61.6%, limiting practical deployment scenarios
Hybrid extension (Section 4.4) orthogonal to main method; improvements come with NFE cost tradeoff, not clearly separable from adaptive samplers
Limited scope: tested on 7-8B parameter models only; applicability to different MDLM architectures beyond LLaDA/Dream/DiffuCoder unclear
